# We tested 12 AI models on hero section design with real users


We mixed 48 AI-made hero sections into the 21st feed and measured which ones developers open.


Alex Smirnov


[@asmirnovxyz](https://x.com/asmirnovxyz)


How often developers opened each model's hero section


% of viewers who opened the model's hero


*Updated results and the full study live at[21st.dev/benchmarks/turing-ui](https://21st.dev/benchmarks/turing-ui) .*


Most design benchmarks show people two outputs and ask them to vote. We ran ours inside the 21st catalog, where developers choose components for their own projects.


## Why copies on 21st are a useful signal


[21st](https://21st.dev/) is a marketplace of React components. You open a component's preview and copy it, most often as a prompt you paste into a coding agent like[Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) or[Cursor](https://cursor.com/) . Copying has a cost. Signed-out visitors have to sign in first, free accounts get two copies a day, and unlimited copying needs a[paid membership](https://21st.dev/pricing) , which more than 10,000 people have.


So a copy means someone chose this component over the others on the page and spent a limited free copy or a paid subscription on it. In effect they vote with money, and they don't know they're voting. The[hero page](https://21st.dev/community/components/s/hero) gets about 48k visitors a month, which is enough traffic to compare models this way.


## The models and the prompt


We used 12 models, each at its highest reasoning setting that still finished the job:


GPT-6.1 Sol


,


GPT-6 Astra


, Claude Fable 5.1


, Claude Opus 5.5


, Claude Sonnet 5.5


, Gemini 3.8 Flash


,


Grok 4.7


,


GLM 5.3


, Qwen 3.8 Max


,


Kimi K3


,


MiMo v2.6 Pro


and Muse Spark 1.3


.


Every model got the same system prompt. It asks for two files in the format 21st publishes (a component and a demo),[React 19](https://react.dev/) with[Tailwind v4](https://tailwindcss.com/) , a short list of allowed libraries ([Framer Motion](https://motion.dev/) ,[GSAP](https://gsap.com/) ,[Three.js](https://threejs.org/) ,[Lucide](https://lucide.dev/) , a few[shadcn/ui](https://ui.shadcn.com/) primitives), no external images, fonts or other URLs, so every visual is drawn in code, and a layout that works from 375 px wide with no console errors.


Each model got one plain API request per brief, with the system prompt and the brief in it. We didn't wrap the models in an agent harness, so a model never saw how its code rendered and couldn't go back to correct it.


Full system prompt


```text
You are building one hero component for the 21st.dev component marketplace.


Output exactly two fenced code blocks and nothing else:
1. `component.tsx` — the reusable component. Start with "use client". Type the props with a Props type. Export the component both as a named export and as default. Accept a `className` prop and merge it with `cn()`. Every prop has a default, so `<Component />` renders the full hero with no props.
2. `demo.tsx` — imports the component from "./component" and renders it full-bleed: wrap it in `min-h-screen w-full` and nothing else. No captions, headings, control panels or "made with" badges in the demo.


Stack: React 19 + TypeScript, Tailwind CSS v4. You may import: react, framer-motion (or motion), gsap, lucide-react, three / @react-three/fiber / @react-three/drei, and standard shadcn/ui primitives from "@/components/ui/<name>" (button, badge, card, input, separator, tabs, sheet, navigation-menu) and `cn` from "@/lib/utils". Anything else must be implemented inside component.tsx.


No external URLs of any kind: no remote images, fonts, videos, 3D models, Spline scenes or CDNs. The preview runs in a sandbox that blocks every cross-origin request, so anything external renders as broken. Draw visuals in code (CSS, SVG, canvas, WebGL), and use plain text for logos.


Theme:
- If the brief says "theme: follows site theme", use only semantic tokens (bg-background, text-foreground, bg-card, text-muted-foreground, border-border, bg-primary, text-primary-foreground, …) or `var(--color-*)`; it must look right in both light and dark. Never write `hsl(var(--x))` or `oklch(var(--x))`.
- If the brief says "theme: dark", the hero paints its own dark background and must look the same whatever the site theme is.


Must work from 375px to 1920px wide with no horizontal scroll. Animations must respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. Give interactive elements stable ids. No console errors.
```


## The four briefs and what the models made


### Ledger


A SaaS product hero (dark):


> Build a hero for "Ledger", invoicing software for freelancers. Headline "Get paid without the chasing", subheadline "Send invoices in seconds, track every payment, and let reminders do the awkward part.", call to action "Start free". Everything else (layout, visuals, colors, typography, motion) is up to you.


### Aurelia


A scroll-expanding media hero (dark):


> Build a hero for "Aurelia", a travel film studio. A framed media panel sits in the center of the first screen with the title "Stories from the edge of the map" split around it. As the user scrolls, the panel grows until it fills the viewport, the two halves of the title slide apart and fade, and the page then continues to a short paragraph: "Twelve films. Six continents. One crew that never stops moving." The media panel is a slow, abstract animated landscape drawn in code. Mood: cinematic, quiet.


### Orbit


An interactive 3D hero (follows the site theme):


> Build a hero for "Orbit", a satellite-data API. Left: eyebrow "Now in public beta", headline "The planet, as an API", subheadline "Query imagery, weather and ground truth for any coordinate in a single call.", buttons "Get an API key" and "Read the docs". Right: an interactive 3D globe or object that slowly rotates and tilts toward the cursor. On mobile the object moves above the text. Mood: precise, technical.


### Nocturne


An atmospheric dark hero:


> Build a hero for "Nocturne", a sleep-sound app. A dark, atmospheric scene with a slow light effect (beams, glow, aurora or stars, your choice) behind very large type: "Fall asleep to something beautiful". Below: "Generative soundscapes that never repeat, tuned to how you breathe." and buttons "Try it free" and "Listen to a sample". Elements reveal in sequence on load. Mood: dreamy, slow, premium.


## Getting a working component out of each model


We rendered every output in a headless browser at 375 and 1440 px, in light and dark mode. A model got another attempt only when its first one didn't work: no code, a crash, or a response cut off mid-stream. The first working attempt is the one that went live. Each model had to return its two files as markdown code blocks, and when a model broke that format the code couldn't be extracted automatically, so we fixed it by hand.

All 48 components ended up working. The cost for one hero ranged from $0.02 (


MiMo


) to $4.53 ( Fable


), and the whole run came to about $50 including failed attempts. More reasoning made the code longer, usually 600 to 1,100 lines, but it didn't make the designs more different from each other.


## How the test works


The 48 sections are published from one neutral studio account with matching covers, and the cards don't show the model. Signed-in visitors to the hero page see two of them in the feed, at positions 6 and 12. Both come from the same brief and from two different models, so every page view is a blind comparison between two models. A random 10% of visitors get the normal feed as a control.


## How the sections did


Cards higher in the feed get opened more, so we compare each AI section with the human card that the control group saw in the same slot. Both sides count only the default view of the hero page, and each member once.

The AI sections hold up against human-made cards: the gap is within noise in both slots. They didn't put people off the page either. The share of visitors who open anything at all is 54% with the inserts and 54% in the control.


The brief made a bigger difference than the slot did.


How often AI-made heroes are opened, by brief


% of viewers who opened an AI-made hero, all 12 models together. Lines: likely range.


Aurelia


's lead is statistically real (p ≈ 0.005). It is also the brief where the models' designs differed the most, while on the other three most models converged on the same layout.


## Which models won


The models do differ overall (p ≈ 0.02 across all twelve), but no single leader is ahead of the rest beyond the margin of error.


We rank the models two ways. Pick rate is the share of members who opened a model's section after seeing it. Take Claude Fable 5.1


: 1,332 members saw at least one of its four sections, and 40 of them opened the one they saw, so its pick rate is 40 / 1,332 = 3.0%. Each member counts once per model. Some briefs get opened more than others and they didn't land evenly across models, so the rates below are adjusted for each model's mix of briefs.


How often developers opened each model's hero


% of viewers who opened the model's hero. Lines: likely range.


Head to head uses only page views where a member saw both sections and opened exactly one: the opened one wins. A Bradley–Terry model turns those wins into ratings on the Elo scale, where 1500 is the average model, and takes out the advantage of sitting in slot 6.


Head-to-head rating


Duel: a viewer saw two AI-made heroes and opened one. 1500 = average model. Lines: likely range.


The two rankings agree at both ends:


GPT-6.1 Sol


is first and


Kimi K3


last on both, and Claude Fable 5.1


is third on both. In the middle they disagree most about Gemini 3.8 Flash

cost $1.50 for its four heroes and Claude Fable 5.1


cost $15.96, and Gemini 3.8 Flash

MiMo v2.6 Pro


and
